strengths: Addresses a timely and underexplored problem: universal, transferable (black-box) adversarial patch attacks against VLA-driven robots, extending prior white-box VLA attacks (e.g., RoboAttack) to realistic threat models where the attacker only has a surrogate.

The framework is technically well-composed and cohesive, combining a feature-space objective (ℓ1 deviation + repulsive InfoNCE), a bi-level robustness-augmented min-max procedure (RUPA), and two VLA-specific losses (Patch Attention Dominance and Patch Semantic Misalignment) that jointly target representation, attention, and semantics.

Empirical transfer results are strong and consistent: in Table 1 the patch drives the simulated average success rate down to 5.75% (from 98.25% benign) and physical to 40.25%, substantially outperforming UMA/UADA/TMA baselines (41-69%) across tasks and viewpoints.

Ablations (Tables 3 and 4) systematically isolate the contribution of each component (RUPA, PAD, PSM, J_tr, L_con, L_1, probe phrasing), supporting the design choices rather than relying on a single end-to-end number.

Evaluation spans multiple VLA families (OpenVLA-7B, OpenVLA-oft variants, π0), simulated LIBERO suites, real-world BridgeData V2 settings, and physical robot execution, with patch visualizations comparing against baseline patterns.

The connection between surrogate feature-space deviation and target displacement is motivated with a proposition (lower-bounded displacement under a linear-alignment assumption) and supported by CCA / linear-probe analysis (R² ≈ 0.654).
weaknesses: The theoretical grounding is thin relative to the strength of the claims: Assumption 1 (existence of a single linear alignment map with bounded residual) is a strong idealization, and its empirical support rests on a single R² ≈ 0.654 value and a CCA probe; the derivation of Proposition 1/Corollary 1 does not tightly characterize when transfer will or will not hold.

The 'universal' claim is stronger than what is demonstrated: the patch is optimized on a specific surrogate and evaluated largely on OpenVLA-family variants and π0; true architectural universality (e.g., very different backbones, RL-tuned policies, diffusion policies beyond π0) is not established.

Physical-world transfer is markedly weaker than simulated (40.25-61.50% average success vs. 5.75-43.50% in simulation), and the improvement over the best baseline in some physical settings (e.g., Table 1 spatial: 26 vs 65-90) is less dramatic; the paper understates this gap.

The inner-loop 'robustness augmentation' is presented as emulating robust training but is a heuristic without formal justification; it is unclear why a bounded sample-wise perturbation faithfully approximates adversarial training of the surrogate rather than simply regularizing the patch.

Patch placement is 'predetermined for each suite to avoid occluding objects,' which may overstate practicality and reproducibility; the effect of placement policy on attack success is not analyzed, and it is not established that the attacker could reliably find such placements in a real deployment.

The novelty relative to prior white-box VLA attacks (RoboAttack, [49]) is incremental—essentially adding transferability machinery and two auxiliary losses—and the paper does not clearly delineate which gains come from transferability versus from stronger white-box optimization.

Some key implementation details and additional transfer results are deferred to a non-visible appendix, limiting reproducibility assessment (e.g., exact loss weights, patch dimensions, probe construction, physical setup).
No defense or mitigation analysis is provided beyond a closing remark about a 'baseline for future defenses,' leaving the practical impact for safety assessment partially unaddressed.

strengths: Targets an important and timely problem: black-box, universal, transferable physical patch attacks on VLA-driven robots, which is directly relevant to safety assessment of embodied policies.

If the headline numbers hold, reducing task success from a benign 98.25% to 5.75% on an unseen fine-tuned victim (OpenVLA-oft-w) would be a strong, practically meaningful demonstration that a single patch can transfer across both model variants and training recipes.

Couples several complementary mechanisms (feature-space ℓ1 deviation, repulsive InfoNCE, bi-level robustness augmentation, PAD, PSM) and reports ablations for each, which at least attempts to isolate the effects of individual components.
Evaluation spans multiple benchmarks (LIBERO, BridgeData V2) and victim families (OpenVLA-oft variants, π0), broadening the scope relative to prior single-model VLA attacks.
Attempts to formalize transferability (Proposition 1, Corollary 1) instead of relying purely on empirical claims, which is a useful direction for this line of work.
weaknesses: The transferability theory is largely decorative. Assumption 1 (target features are a linear function of surrogate features plus bounded residual) is strong and never empirically validated; the reported R²≈0.654 means a single linear map only explains ~65% of the target variance, and ε_E is never estimated, so the bound in Prop. 1 can be vacuous. The step from a lower bound to Corollary 1's 'necessarily induces a nontrivial increase' does not follow.

Novelty is incremental: ℓ1 feature deviations, InfoNCE repulsion, PGD inner-min/outer-max robustness augmentation, and attention steering are all borrowed from prior work; the components are combined in a largely ad hoc manner, and the 'first universal, transferable patch attack' claim is overstated given that [49]'s objectives are already universal patch attacks.

Ablation results (Tab. 3) are within noise: removing RUPA (62.25), PAD (62.50), or PSM (63.50) changes the average success rate from the full model (61.50) by only 0.75–2.0 points, yet the text claims they 'consistently weaken the attack.' No variance or confidence intervals are reported even though each suite involves only 100 rollouts, so these differences are unlikely to be significant.

Tab. 3 is internally inconsistent: removing the entire feature objective (w/o Jtr, 85.75%) is dramatically worse than removing L1 alone (64.00%) or Lcon alone (70.75%), which does not follow if Jtr = L1 + λ_con Lcon. This suggests the ablation protocol or labeling is not what is described.

There is a large, unexplained discrepancy between Tab. 1 and Tab. 2 for the same attack and same surrogate: 'Our' falls from 61.50 to 43.50 in the simulated setting and from 40.25 to 61.50 in the physical setting. Baselines shift similarly. This raises serious questions about result stability and comparability across the two experiments that the manuscript does not address.

The 'Simulated' and 'Physical' blocks of Tabs. 1 and 2 have identical benign success rates (99/99/98/97 and 98/98/98/94, respectively). Either the two blocks are not actually distinct conditions or there is a copy-paste error; the manuscript never defines clearly what 'physical' means (real robot vs. different training data in the same simulator).

The manuscript is incomplete: multiple 'Appendix ??' references, a broken proof reference ('app:app:app:app:...'), missing implementation/patch-size/ε/iteration details, and reliance on an unavailable appendix for white-box results and hyperparameter sensitivity. Many key claims cannot be verified from the submitted text.

Notation and definitions are sloppy: σ is used both for the sample-wise perturbation and (as σ_min) for singular values; D vs d vs D_t dimension symbols are inconsistent; Eq. 11 applies x + σ over the whole image while Section 3.4 also states the perturbation is 'confined to the patch mask,' a direct contradiction. The role and radius ε_σ are never justified or ablated.

A large number of hyperparameters (λ_con, λ_PAD, λ_PSM, α, β, τ, margin m, top-ρ, ε_σ, I, K) are introduced with essentially no justification, sensitivity analysis, or budget comparison to the baselines. The reported gains could partly reflect additional optimization capacity rather than the design claims.

The security and 'sim-to-real' framing is stronger than the evidence supports: physical results appear to be only a different training-data regime rather than genuine real-robot execution, and no deployment details (patch printing, mounting, camera variability, lighting) are provided, despite the abstract's emphasis on physical execution and sim-to-real shifts.

strengths: Addresses an important and under-explored problem: universal, transferable adversarial patches against VLA-driven robots under strict black-box conditions (unseen architectures, fine-tuned variants, and sim-to-real shifts), which is a meaningful step beyond prior white-box VLA attack work.

Proposes a coherent, unified framework (UPA-RFAS) that integrates a feature-space objective (L1 deviation + repulsive InfoNCE), a robustness-augmented two-phase min-max procedure (RAUP), and two VLA-specific losses (Patch Attention Dominance and Patch Semantic Misalignment), each with a clear rationale.

Provides a theoretical motivation (Assumption 1, Proposition 1, Corollary 1) linking surrogate-side feature deviation to target-side displacement, which gives principled justification for the feature-space design rather than a purely heuristic attack.

Empirical evidence is broad and strong: large drops in success rate (~92 points in the simulated setting), transfer across multiple VLA families (OpenVLA variants and π0), both simulated and real-world-data settings, and informative ablations (Tab. 3, Tab. 4) that isolate the contribution of each component and of probe phrasing.
Patch pattern analysis (Fig. 2) qualitatively contrasts the learned universal patch with baseline artifacts, supporting the claim of model-agnostic transfer over surrogate-specific overfitting.
weaknesses: The theoretical foundation rests on Assumption 1 (linear alignment with bounded residual), which is strong and only moderately supported empirically: the paper reports R^2 ≈ 0.654, yet also asserts 'near-unity Canonical Correlations.' This tension between a moderate R^2 and the claimed near-unity alignment is not reconciled, weakening the strength of the transferability argument.

Proposition 1 and Corollary 1 are relatively direct consequences of the assumption (maximizing L1 deviation increases target displacement via singular-value bounds), so the theoretical contribution is modest and closer to a formal restatement than a deep result.

The 'physical' setting uses models trained on real-world data (BridgeData V2) rather than an actual physical robot deployment; the abstract's phrasing about 'physical executions' risks overstating the evaluation and does not demonstrate real hardware behavior.
No evaluation against defenses or mitigation is provided, so the practical threat and the robustness of the attack to detection/patch-removal are unaddressed despite the safety framing.
Patch placement sites are described as predetermined per suite, which may limit the claimed universality and could make results sensitive to placement choices not fully explored.
Reproducibility is partially limited: key implementation details, evaluation protocols, and additional transfer results are deferred to an appendix not included in the provided material.

strengths: Presents the first systematic study of universal, transferable adversarial patch attacks on VLA-driven robots, addressing a practically important black-box threat model where existing patches overfit to a single model.

Comprehensive empirical evaluation across multiple VLA models (OpenVLA-7B, OpenVLA-oft variants, π0), LIBERO simulated suites, and physical/sim-to-real settings; e.g., transferring from OpenVLA-7B to OpenVLA-oft-w reduces simulated success from 98.25% to 5.75% and physical success from 97.00% to 40.25%, substantially outperforming UMA/UADA/TMA baselines.

The proposed UPA-RFAS method is technically well-motivated, combining feature-space L1 deviation, repulsive contrastive regularization, robustness-augmented bi-level min-max optimization, and VLA-specific Patch Attention Dominance and Patch Semantic Misalignment losses.

Ablation studies (Tables 2-3, 6-8) verify the contribution of each component: removing the full feature-space objective degrades attack to 85.75% avg success, while L_con and L1 terms also matter; patch-size and probe-phrasing ablations provide useful design insights.

Theoretical analysis (Assumption 1, Proposition 1) gives a lower bound linking surrogate feature deviation to target deviation under a linear alignment assumption, and empirical CCA (R^2≈0.654) supports shared representation structure.
Detailed implementation hyperparameters in Appendix B and algorithm pseudocode aid reproducibility; patch pattern analysis shows the method avoids object-mimicking artifacts of baselines.
weaknesses: The linear alignment assumption (Assumption 1) with bounded residual is strong and only empirically quantified for one surrogate-target pair (R^2≈0.654); it may not hold for architecturally distant policies such as π0, limiting theoretical guarantees.

Real-world physical evaluation is largely qualitative (three tasks, three trials, videos in Appendix F) without quantitative success rates in the main paper; broader physical validation is needed to fully support sim-to-real claims.

Baseline comparison is limited to RoboticAttack objectives (UMA/UADA/TMA); other universal or transferable attack methods from the adversarial robustness literature are not compared, and it is unclear whether baselines are optimized for cross-model transfer.

Some notation/sign conventions are confusing (e.g., inner minimization of J_tr = L1 + λ L_con versus the stated goal of maximizing L1 deviation; the PAD/PSM sign choices) and the abstract contains an incomplete code URL ('Code is at .'), reducing clarity/reproducibility.

The RUPA component yields only a modest ablation gain (61.50 vs. 62.25 avg success in Table 2), and the text-probe anchors are manually specified, which may limit generality across tasks and languages.
Potential ethical/safety implications of robot-targeted adversarial patches are not discussed, nor are defenses or mitigations beyond a brief mention of establishing a baseline for future defenses.

strengths: Addresses a timely and safety-relevant problem: black-box/transferable adversarial patch attacks on Vision-Language-Action robots, an area that is genuinely underexplored relative to white-box VLA attacks.

The framework is formulated cleanly (Definition 1, bi-level objective in Eq. 11, Algorithm 1) with full implementation and hyperparameter details (patch 50x50, I=8, K=50, 2000 iterations, loss weights), which supports reproducibility.

The experimental sweep is broad for a first study: two surrogates (OpenVLA-7B, OpenVLA-7B-LIBERO-Long), multiple victims (OpenVLA-oft variants, OpenVLA-oft-w, and π0), simulated and real-data-trained settings, plus ablations on patch size, λ_con, and ε.

The simulated black-box transfer results are strong: on OpenVLA-oft-w the attack drops success from 98.25% (benign) to 5.75%, far below the RoboAttack baselines (41.25–69.25%), and the ablation/hyperparameter studies are informative about patch size and the contrastive term.
weaknesses: Novelty is largely incremental: the core machinery (EOT-style randomized placement, feature-space ℓ1 deviation, InfoNCE repulsion, and an adversarial-training-style bi-level min-max inner loop) is well-established transfer-attack tooling repurposed for VLA. The genuinely VLA-specific pieces (PAD and PSM) contribute only ~1–2 points in Table 2 (w/o PAD 62.50, w/o PSM 63.50 vs. full 61.50), which is within plausible run-to-run noise since no error bars are reported in the main tables.

The theory is weak and partly overclaimed. Assumption 1 posits a linear surrogate→target map with bounded residual, yet the empirical support is only R²≈0.654, which indicates a substantial nonlinear residual and does not justify treating the alignment as near-invertible. More seriously, Corollary 1 states that increasing ||Δz_i||_1 'necessarily induces a nontrivial increase of ||Δg_i||_1', but Eq. 8 is only a lower bound on ||Δg_i||_1; raising a lower bound does not imply the quantity itself increases. The analysis therefore does not logically support the ℓ1 design.

The real-world claim is not supported by the evidence. Appendix F reports only 3 tasks × 3 qualitative trials with no quantitative success rates, and the 'Physical' column in Table 1 is a model trained on BridgeData v2, not a physical robot. The abstract/introduction framing ('real-world settings', 'physical executions', 'sim-to-real') overstates what is actually shown.

The 'universal/model-agnostic' claim is only weakly supported outside the OpenVLA family. On π0 (Table 5) the method beats the best baseline by only 2.5 (sim) and 5.5 (phys) points, and the headline gains are concentrated in OpenVLA-oft variants that share the surrogate's lineage. Cross-architecture transfer is explicitly described as 'substantially harder' and yields modest margins.

White-box performance is not a differentiator: Table 4 shows UDA1-3 already reaches 0.0 average success while the proposed method reaches 0.5/2.75, so the entire case rests on transferability, which is only compared against RoboAttack objectives. No comparison is made to other established transfer-attack families (e.g., feature-disruptive, neuron-attribution, or the cited model-agnostic VLA attack [67]), so the source of the transfer gains is not attributable.

Several claims are overstated relative to the evidence, e.g., 'first to investigate black-box transfer vulnerabilities of VLAs in real-world settings' and 'establishing a strong baseline for future defenses', and the abstract contains a broken artifact ('Code is at .'), indicating incomplete preparation.

strengths: Addresses a timely and important safety problem: universal, transferable physical patch attacks on VLA-driven robots under black-box conditions, a setting that is underexplored relative to white-box VLA attacks.

Proposes a coherent and well-motivated framework, UPA-RFAS, that combines a feature-space L1 deviation objective, repulsive InfoNCE contrastive regularization, a robustness-augmented bi-level optimization (RUPA), and VLA-specific PAD/PSM losses.

Empirical results are strong: black-box transfer from OpenVLA-7B to OpenVLA-oft-w reduces simulated success from 98.25% to 5.75% and physical success to 40.25%, substantially outperforming UMA/UADA/TMA baselines; white-box results in the appendix also nearly zero out success.

Provides theoretical motivation via a linear feature-alignment assumption and a lower-bound proposition linking surrogate-side feature deviations to target-side deviations, supported by CCA/linear-regression analysis.

Evaluation is reasonably broad for an attack paper: LIBERO and BridgeData V2, simulated and physical/real-world-data victim settings, multiple baselines, pi0 transfer in the appendix, ablations on RUPA/PAD/PSM, patch size, probe phrasing, and epsilon/lambda sensitivity.
Patch visualizations and analysis suggest the learned universal patch avoids object/scene-specific mimicry that hurts baseline patches, offering some insight into why transfer improves.
The paper is generally well organized, with clear equations, algorithm pseudocode, and implementation details that support reproducibility.
weaknesses: Statistical significance is not established for several key claims: main and ablation tables report point success rates without variance or confidence intervals, and ablations for RUPA/PAD/PSM show only 1–2 point average differences, making the claim that each component 'consistently' weakens the attack hard to verify.

There is a hyperparameter inconsistency: the implementation uses epsilon = 2/255 for the inner perturbation, but Table 8 indicates epsilon = 4/255 gives the best attack (58.00% average success vs. 61.50%), and the text itself argues moderate epsilon = 4/255 is best. The main experiments therefore appear to use a suboptimal setting, weakening the RUPA design justification.

Victim diversity is more limited than claimed: the text says transfer is evaluated to four different OpenVLA-oft variants, but Table 1 shows only two victim columns (OpenVLA-oft-w and OpenVLA-oft). Broader VLA architectures such as Octo are not quantitatively tested, and the pi0 transfer in the appendix shows smaller margins, so universality across truly heterogeneous VLA families is not fully demonstrated.

The 'physical' evaluation is ambiguous and potentially overclaimed: the main tables' physical setting likely refers to models trained on real-world data but evaluated in LIBERO simulation, while actual robot experiments are qualitative only (3 tasks x 3 trials, no quantitative success rate). The conclusion's sim-to-real claim is therefore stronger than the main quantitative evidence supports.

Theoretical Assumption 1 is strong and only empirically supported by CCA/R^2 ≈ 0.654 for one surrogate-victim pair; the residual bound epsilon_E is not estimated. The guarantee from Proposition 1 may be loose in practice and does not fully explain transfer across very different architectures.

The PAD and PSM losses are architecture- and prompt-specific: PAD relies on OpenVLA-style text-to-vision attention maps, and PSM uses hand-designed probe phrases. Their marginal ablation gains (e.g., w/o PSM 63.50 vs. full 61.50) suggest limited individual impact, and generalization to other VLA attention structures is not deeply analyzed.

Reproducibility is slightly hindered by an incomplete code URL in the abstract ('Code is at .') and by the lack of quantitative protocols for the real-world robot trials, although the method section and appendix are otherwise detailed.
